Airbus HMI

Overview

One interface for the flight deck and the loadmaster, built on a single alert language, visible safety margins and deliberate confirmation.

The brief

Case study

The A350F made its first flight from Toulouse on 29 September 2026. Airbus is running a flight-test programme of around 400 hours, with certification and first customer deliveries planned for the second half of 2027. This concept asks what its crew and loadmaster would need on screen if the interface were designed around one shared grammar instead of a collection of system pages.

Two users share one aircraft. The pilot needs to read state fast and act without error. The loadmaster needs to see a numeric limit become a physical consequence. The same alert, the same confirmation and the same balance bar serve both. The simulated flight is Paris Charles de Gaulle to Delhi, started from a cold and dark aircraft.

Other details that shaped the interface: six interchangeable touchscreen displays, a cabin altitude of 6,000 ft, cargo air flows segregated from the crew areas with cargo temperature control down to 4 °C, and a floor designed for flexible pallet loading and centre of gravity management.

    The door

    The feature operators asked for.

    Airbus describes the A350F's main deck cargo door as the largest in the industry: a 175 in (4,445 mm) cut-out with a 169.5 in (4,305 mm) clear opening, electrically operated and placed behind the wing so the main deck and lower deck can be loaded at the same time. It is sized so large jet engines can be loaded without disassembly.

    The HMI gives it its own element. A door card shows the state in words and colour, lists the interlocks that must be met (on the ground, engines shut down) and asks for a hold to open. The same door appears highlighted in the plan view, the 3D cutaway and a true-scale cross-section, where it is drawn against a 125 in pallet.

    Principles

    Each one is visible in the demo above.

    One alert grammar

    A tier is always a colour, a shape and a word together. Flight, fuel and cargo raise alerts into the same stack, so a loadmaster's CG warning reads exactly like a pilot's fuel caution.

    Show the margin, not only the value

    The speed tape carries a coloured margin strip and a distance-to-limit chip. The CG envelope shows a caution band and the path from empty aircraft to the current load.

    Slow down irreversible actions

    Selecting descent, discharging an extinguishing agent and locking a manifest all use the same hold-to-confirm control. Reversible changes stay one tap.

    Borrow from the best interfaces

    Flight simulators like Microsoft Flight Simulator treat the cockpit tablet as a set of small apps, and keep checklists beside live state. Here, checklists live inside the alert that triggers them, and the six-screen layout lets a crew move a briefing from one screen to another in a single action.

    Reuse components across systems

    The balance bar measures fuel left to right and lane load left to right. The segmented arc shows thrust and the loading gauge. Learn one, read both.

    Four more screens

    Each one answers a question the crew asks at a specific moment.

    Approach and landing

    Deviation is shown as two dots each way and turns green only when both beams are captured. Flare and retard appear as words at the radio altitudes where they matter, and the five configuration items sit beside them so nothing is hunted for.

    Checklist

    An alert tells the crew what is wrong. The checklist tells them what to do next, one step per row, with a progress bar. Ticking the crossfeed step really opens the valve, so the procedure and the aircraft stay in agreement.

    Manifest and dangerous goods

    The list, the deck plan and the envelope read the same data. A dangerous goods mark adds an amber diamond to the pallet and blocks locking if two are placed side by side.

    Diversion

    Distance alone is not enough on a long sector, so each alternate shows time, fuel needed and fuel left. Switching to one engine out changes speed and burn and redraws every ring.

    Component library

    Live instances, not screenshots.

    Alert tiers

    Colour, shape and label always travel together, so no tier depends on colour alone.

    Hold to confirm

    1.2 seconds, cancelable by release. Works with pointer, touch and the space bar.

    Rotary dial

    Drag in a circle, scroll, or use arrow keys. Shift or Page keys move in tens.

    Value 40

    Segmented arc

    A white fill with amber and red zones, and a cyan tick for the commanded value.

    Balance bar

    Zero sits at the centre. Zones are drawn on the track so the limit is visible before it is reached.

    Segmented switch and toggle

    A sliding thumb shows which mode is live. The toggle always spells out its state.

    Colour has a job

    Follows the long-standing alerting hierarchy in cockpit certification rules (CS-25.1322): red for warnings, amber for cautions.
    RedWarning. Act now.#FF5A5D
    AmberCaution. Act soon, or a margin is shrinking.#FFB62E
    CyanSelected or armed by the crew. Also the interactive accent.#3AD4EC
    GreenActive mode, or a value inside limits.#4BE38F
    MagentaThe planned route.#E676F0
    WhiteCurrent values. Everything else stays quiet.#E8EEF6

    Sources and limits

    • Airbus: A350F product page (figures taken from a saved copy supplied by the author)
    • Aerospace Global News report on the A350F first flight (supplied by the author)
    • Aviation News: A350F completes maiden flight
    • Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024: adding an EFB, for the app-style cockpit tablet idea
    • MSFS 2024 EFB guide

    Weights, centre of gravity limits, fuel quantities, engine figures, wind and the flight itself are invented for the simulation. An earlier Airbus infographic quotes a 172 in door; the product page lists 175 in cut-out and 169.5 in clear opening, so this page uses the product page. Speeds use standard-atmosphere maths (indicated airspeed to Mach, true airspeed and ground speed); the overspeed and stall limits on the tape are simulated. The layout draws on the ideas behind ARINC 661 but is not an implementation of it.
